nameStory: The Golden-tailed Leafcutter Bee gets its name from the distinctive golden or yellowish hairs on its abdomen that catch the light beautifully when it flies. Like all leafcutter bees, it's called a 'leafcutter' because it uses its strong mandibles (jaws) to cut neat circular pieces from leaves to build its nest cells. The scientific name 'relativa' means 'related' in Latin, suggesting it was recognized as being closely related to other known leafcutter species when first described in 1878.
description: The Golden-tailed Leafcutter Bee is a solitary bee about the size of a honeybee, typically measuring around half an inch long. It has a robust, somewhat cylindrical body with dark coloration and distinctive golden or yellowish hairs on its tail end (abdomen). Like other leafcutter bees, it carries pollen on the underside of its abdomen rather than on its legs, giving it a distinctive fuzzy-bellied appearance when loaded with pollen. These industrious bees are excellent pollinators that work alone rather than in colonies.

idTips.label: Golden tail hairs
idTips.description: Look for distinctive golden or yellowish hairs on the tip of the abdomen that shimmer in sunlight and contrast with the darker body color

idTips.label: Pollen basket location
idTips.description: Watch for bright orange or yellow pollen carried on the underside of the abdomen (called a scopa) rather than on the legs like honeybees

idTips.label: Body shape and size
idTips.description: Notice the robust, cylindrical body about the size of a honeybee but stockier, with a somewhat rectangular appearance when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Observe the direct, purposeful flight style as it moves between flowers or carries leaf pieces back to nesting sites

idTips.label: Leaf-cutting behavior
idTips.description: Watch for the distinctive behavior of cutting neat, circular pieces from rose, lilac, or other soft-leaved plants with audible snipping sounds

habitat: Golden-tailed Leafcutter Bees prefer sunny, open areas with access to both flowers and suitable nesting sites. They're often found in gardens, meadows, forest edges, and suburban areas where they can find soft-leaved plants for nest construction. They typically nest in existing cavities like hollow plant stems, old beetle holes in wood, or gaps in stone walls and buildings.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with males appearing first followed by females who start seeking nesting sites and flowers for nectar.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you'll see them actively cutting leaves, visiting flowers, and provisioning nest cells with pollen balls for their young.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down as the generation completes development, with new adults preparing to overwinter as mature larvae or pupae in their nest cells.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity visible; next generation develops slowly in protected nest cells, waiting for spring warmth to emerge.

funFact: A single female Golden-tailed Leafcutter Bee can cut over 1,000 perfectly circular leaf pieces during her lifetime, each piece cut with the precision of a cookie cutter, and she arranges them like overlapping shingles to create waterproof nursery cells for her babies!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Megachile leafcutter bees, but the golden tail hairs are distinctive. Remember: 'Golden tail tells the tale' - look for those shimmery golden hairs on the abdomen tip that other dark leafcutter bees lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'leafcutter' bees, they don't damage plants significantly - they're actually beneficial pollinators that take only small amounts of leaf material. The circular cuts they make in leaves are often mistaken for plant disease or pest damage by gardeners.
compareHints: Among New England's many Megachile species, the Golden-tailed Leafcutter Bee stands out with its distinctive golden abdominal hairs, while relatives like the Black-and-gray Leafcutter Bee have contrasting gray and black coloration instead. The similar-sized Patchwork Leafcutter Bee has white hair patches rather than golden ones. Most other regional Megachile species are either larger (like the introduced Sculptured Resin Bee) or have different hair color patterns entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the leafcutter bees in its genus that cut neat circular pieces from leaves, the Sculptured Resin Bee collects sticky tree resins and other plant materials for nest construction.
Among New England's leafcutter bees, males of this species are easily distinguished by their notably broad front legs - most other Megachile males have normal-width legs.
Among New England's many Megachile species, the Alfalfa Leafcutter Bee is distinguished by its agricultural associations and widespread management by farmers.

Among New England's many Megachile species, the Flat-tailed Leafcutter's compressed abdomen sets it apart from relatives like the Alfalfa Leafcutter Bee and Patchwork Leafcutter Bee, which have more typically rounded abdomens.
Unlike the leaf-cutting members of its genus like the patchwork leafcutter bee, the bellflower resin bee works exclusively with sticky materials and never cuts leaf pieces.
Among New England's leafcutter bees, the Pugnacious stands out for its completely black coloration and larger size - most relatives have some lighter markings or metallic hints.
Compared to other Megachile species, unarmed leafcutter bees are distinguished by the males' lack of prominent facial or leg spines that many relatives possess.
